title: 2-factor theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $G$ be a regular graph whose degree is an even number, $2k$ . Then the edges of $G$ can be partitioned into $k$ edge-disjoint 2-factors.
statement: Every finite $2k$-regular graph $G$ has an edge partition into $k$ edge-disjoint 2-factors.
hypotheses: $G$ is a finite $2k$-regular graph, with $k$ a nonnegative integer.
conclusions: The edge set of $G$ can be partitioned into $k$ edge-disjoint spanning 2-regular subgraphs.
editorial_note: Retains 2-factor definition from adjacent excerpt.

title: Absorption (logic)
source_statement_excerpt: Absorption is a valid argument form and rule of inference of propositional logic. The rule states that if $P$ implies $Q$ , then $P$ implies $P$ and $Q$ . The rule makes it possible to introduce conjunctions to proofs. It is called the law of absorption because the term $Q$ is "absorbed" by the term $P$ in the consequent. The rule can be stated: ${\frac {P\to Q}{\therefore P\to (P\land Q)}}$ where the rule is that wherever an instance of " $P\to Q$ " appears on a line of a proof, " $P\to (P\land Q)$ " can be placed on a subsequent line.
statement: For propositions $P,Q$, $(P\to Q)\to(P\to(P\land Q))$ is a tautology.
hypotheses: $P$ and $Q$ are propositions; assume $P\to Q$.
conclusions: $P\to(P\land Q)$.
editorial_note: Propositional absorption rule; selected inference rather than surrounding exposition.

title: Alexander's subbase lemma
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, specifically topology, Alexander's subbase lemma states that for a topological space to be a compact, it is necessary and sufficient that each open cover of the space consisting of sets in a (fixed) subbase has a finite subcover. Precisely,
statement: A topological space $X$ is compact if and only if every cover of $X$ by members of a fixed subbase of its topology admits a finite subcover.
hypotheses: $X$ is a topological space and $\mathcal S$ is a subbase for its topology.
conclusions: $X$ is compact if and only if every $\mathcal S$-cover of $X$ has a finite subcover.
editorial_note: Selected main whole-space version; source has incomplete displayed material concerning subsets.

title: Angle bisector theorem
source_statement_excerpt: The generalized angle bisector theorem (which is not necessarily an angle bisector theorem, since the angle ∠ A is not necessarily bisected into equal parts) states that if D lies on the line BC, then
statement: In triangle $ABC$, for $D$ on side $BC$, the line $AD$ bisects $\angle BAC$ if and only if $|BD|/|CD|=|AB|/|AC|$.
hypotheses: $ABC$ is a nondegenerate triangle and $D$ lies in the interior of side $BC$.
conclusions: $AD$ bisects $\angle BAC$ if and only if $\frac{|BD|}{|CD|}=\frac{|AB|}{|AC|}$.
editorial_note: Uses main theorem and converse present in adjacent paragraphs; omits generalized variant.

title: Area theorem (conformal mapping)
source_statement_excerpt: Suppose that $f$ is analytic and injective in the punctured open unit disk $\mathbb {D} \setminus \{0\}$ and has the power series representation
statement: If $f(z)=z^{-1}+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nz^n$ is analytic and injective on the punctured unit disk, then $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n|a_n|^2\le1$.
hypotheses: $f$ is analytic and injective on $\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}$ and has Laurent expansion $f(z)=1/z+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nz^n$.
conclusions: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n|a_n|^2\le 1$.
editorial_note: Following displayed formula in source excerpt supplies conclusion.

title: Artin–Tate lemma
source_statement_excerpt: The lemma is similar to the Eakin–Nagata theorem, which says: if C is finite over B and C is a Noetherian ring, then B is a Noetherian ring.
editorial_note: Source extractor omits the statement of the Artin–Tate lemma and only includes a comparison with Eakin–Nagata.

title: Atiyah–Singer index theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In differential geometry, the Atiyah–Singer index theorem, proved by Michael Atiyah and Isadore Singer (1963), states that for an elliptic differential operator on a compact manifold, the analytical index (related to the dimension of the space of solutions) is equal to the topological index (defined in terms of some topological data). It includes many other theorems, such as the Chern–Gauss–Bonnet theorem and Riemann–Roch theorem, as special cases, and has applications to theoretical physics.
statement: The analytic index of an elliptic differential operator on a compact manifold equals its topological index.
hypotheses: $D$ is an elliptic differential operator on a compact manifold, with analytic and topological indices defined.
conclusions: $\operatorname{ind}_{\mathrm{analytic}}D=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathrm{topological}}D$.
editorial_note: Principal index equality from lead; no extra proof or refinements.

title: Ax–Kochen theorem
source_statement_excerpt: The Ax–Kochen theorem, named for James Ax and Simon B. Kochen, states that for each positive integer d there is a finite set Yd of prime numbers, such that if p is any prime not in Yd then every homogeneous polynomial of degree d over the p-adic numbers in at least d2 + 1 variables has a nontrivial zero.
statement: For every positive integer $d$ there is a finite set $Y_d$ of primes such that every homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$ over $\mathbb Q_p$ in at least $d^2+1$ variables has a nontrivial zero whenever $p\notin Y_d$.
hypotheses: $d$ is a positive integer; $p$ is a prime outside the finite exceptional set $Y_d$; $F$ is homogeneous of degree $d$ over $\mathbb Q_p$ in at least $d^2+1$ variables.
conclusions: $F$ has a nonzero solution over $\mathbb Q_p$.
editorial_note: Preserves source's quantification of finite exceptional set by degree.

title: Baire category theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Versions of the Baire category theorem were first proved independently in 1897 by Osgood for the real line $\mathbb {R} $ and in 1899 by Baire for Euclidean space $\mathbb {R} ^{n}$ . The more general statement for completely metrizable spaces was first shown by Hausdorff in 1914.
statement: Every completely metrizable space is a Baire space, and every locally compact Hausdorff space is a Baire space.
hypotheses: $X$ is a topological space that is either completely metrizable or locally compact Hausdorff.
conclusions: Every countable intersection of dense open subsets of $X$ is dense in $X$.
editorial_note: Two independently sufficient cases, with generalizations to pseudometric/regular spaces also noted in source.

hypotheses: $X$ is completely metrizable.
conclusions: $X$ is a Baire space.

hypotheses: $X$ is locally compact Hausdorff.
conclusions: $X$ is a Baire space.

title: Banach–Tarski paradox
source_statement_excerpt: The Banach–Tarski paradox is a theorem in set-theoretic geometry that states the following: Given a solid ball in three-dimensional space, there exists a decomposition of the ball into a finite number of disjoint subsets that can be put back together in a different way to yield two identical copies of the original ball. Indeed, the reassembly process involves only moving the pieces around and rotating them, without changing their original shape. The pieces themselves are not "solids" in the traditional sense, but infinite scatterings of points. The reconstruction can work with as few as five pieces.
statement: A solid ball in three-dimensional Euclidean space can be partitioned into finitely many disjoint subsets which, using only rigid motions, can be reassembled into two copies of the original ball.
hypotheses: $B$ is a solid ball in $\mathbb R^3$.
conclusions: There is a finite partition of $B$ whose pieces can be moved by translations and rotations to form two disjoint balls each congruent to $B$.
editorial_note: Records main equidecomposition statement; no claim pieces are measurable.

title: Beatty sequence
source_statement_excerpt: Rayleigh's theorem, named after Lord Rayleigh, states that the complement of a Beatty sequence, consisting of the positive integers that are not in the sequence, is itself a Beatty sequence generated by a different irrational number.
statement: If $r>1$ is irrational and $s=r/(r-1)$, then the Beatty sequences $\{\lfloor nr\rfloor:n\ge1\}$ and $\{\lfloor ns\rfloor:n\ge1\}$ partition the positive integers.
hypotheses: $r>1$ is irrational; $s=r/(r-1)$.
conclusions: Every positive integer belongs to exactly one of $\{\lfloor nr\rfloor:n\ge1\}$ and $\{\lfloor ns\rfloor:n\ge1\}$.
editorial_note: Adjacent definition gives the complementary parameter explicitly.

title: Behnke–Stein theorem on Stein manifolds
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, especially several complex variables, the Behnke–Stein theorem states that a connected, non-compact (open) Riemann surface is a Stein manifold. In other words, it states that there is a nonconstant single-valued holomorphic function (univalent function) on such a Riemann surface. It is a generalization of the Runge approximation theorem and was proved by Heinrich Behnke and Karl Stein in 1948.
statement: Every connected noncompact Riemann surface is a Stein manifold.
hypotheses: $X$ is a connected noncompact Riemann surface.
conclusions: $X$ is a Stein manifold.
editorial_note: Uses the principal precise characterization; avoids weaker explanatory paraphrase.

title: Bertrand's ballot theorem
source_statement_excerpt: ${\frac {p-q}{p+q}}.$
statement: In a uniformly random order of $p$ votes for candidate $A$ and $q$ votes for candidate $B$, with $p>q$, the probability that $A$ is strictly ahead throughout the count is $(p-q)/(p+q)$.
hypotheses: $p,q$ are nonnegative integers with $p>q$; the $p+q$ ballots consist of $p$ votes for $A$ and $q$ for $B$ and are counted in a uniformly random order.
conclusions: $\Pr(A\text{ has strictly more votes than }B\text{ after every ballot})=\frac{p-q}{p+q}$.
editorial_note: Uses problem statement adjacent to isolated formula.

title: Binomial sum variance inequality
source_statement_excerpt: Consider the sum, Z, of two independent binomial random variables, X ~ B(m0, p0) and Y ~ B(m1, p1), where Z = X + Y. Then, the variance of Z is less than or equal to its variance under the assumption that p0 = p1 = ${\bar {p}}$ , that is, if Z had a binomial distribution with the success probability equal to the average of X and Y 's probabilities. Symbolically, $Var(Z)\leqslant E[Z](1-{\tfrac {E[Z]}{m_{0}+m_{1}}})$ .
statement: For independent $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(m_0,p_0)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Bin}(m_1,p_1)$, $Z=X+Y$ satisfies $\operatorname{Var}(Z)\le \mathbb E[Z]\bigl(1-\mathbb E[Z]/(m_0+m_1)\bigr)$.
hypotheses: $X,Y$ are independent, $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(m_0,p_0)$, $Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(m_1,p_1)$, $m_0+m_1>0$ and $Z=X+Y$.
conclusions: $\operatorname{Var}(Z)\le \mathbb E[Z]\left(1-\frac{\mathbb E[Z]}{m_0+m_1}\right)$.
editorial_note: Retains stated variance inequality without introducing an unverified equality characterization.

title: Blichfeldt's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: The theorem can be stated most simply for points in the Euclidean plane, and for the integer lattice in the plane. For this version of the theorem, let $S$ be any bounded and measurable set, let $A$ denote its area, and round this number up to the next integer value, $n=\lceil A\rceil $ . Then Blichfeldt's theorem states that $S$ can be translated so that its translated copy contains at least $n$ points with integer coordinates.
statement: If $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ is bounded and measurable with area $A$, some translate of $S$ contains at least $\lceil A\rceil$ integer lattice points.
hypotheses: $S\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is bounded and measurable, and $A$ is its Lebesgue area.
conclusions: There exists $t\in\mathbb R^2$ such that $|(S+t)\cap\mathbb Z^2|\ge\lceil A\rceil$.
editorial_note: Follows the planar formulation explicitly provided.

title: Bohr–Mollerup theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematical analysis, the Bohr–Mollerup theorem is a theorem proved by the Danish mathematicians Harald Bohr and Johannes Mollerup. The theorem characterizes the gamma function, defined for x > 0 by
statement: The gamma function is the unique positive log-convex function $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ satisfying $f(1)=1$ and $f(x+1)=xf(x)$ for all $x>0$.
hypotheses: $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is logarithmically convex, satisfies $f(1)=1$, and $f(x+1)=xf(x)$ for every $x>0$.
conclusions: $f(x)=\Gamma(x)=\int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ for all $x>0$.
editorial_note: All three uniqueness conditions and integral definition taken from adjacent source.

title: Borel–Cantelli lemma
source_statement_excerpt: The first Borel–Cantelli lemma, which states that if the sum of the probabilities of the events is finite, then the probability that infinitely many of them occur is 0. This result holds for any sequence of events, without additional assumptions;
statement: If $(A_n)$ is a sequence of events with $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\Pr(A_n)<\infty$, then $\Pr(A_n\text{ infinitely often})=0$.
hypotheses: $(A_n)_{n\ge1}$ is a sequence of events in a probability space and $\sum_n\Pr(A_n)<\infty$.
conclusions: $\Pr(\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n)=0$.
editorial_note: First Borel–Cantelli lemma only; no independence requirement.

title: Bott periodicity theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, the Bott periodicity theorem describes a periodicity in the homotopy groups of classical groups, discovered by Raoul Bott (1957, 1959), which proved to be of foundational significance for much further research, in particular in K-theory of stable complex vector bundles, as well as the stable homotopy groups of spheres. Bott periodicity can be formulated in numerous ways, with the periodicity in question always appearing as a period-2 phenomenon, with respect to dimension, for the theory associated to the unitary group. See for example topological K-theory.
statement: For the stable unitary group $U(\infty)=\varinjlim_n U(n)$, $\pi_i(U(\infty))\cong\pi_{i+2}(U(\infty))$ for all $i\ge0$, with $\pi_0=0$ and $\pi_1\cong\mathbb Z$.
hypotheses: $U(\infty)$ is the direct limit of unitary groups $U(n)$; $i\ge0$.
conclusions: $\pi_i(U(\infty))\cong\pi_{i+2}(U(\infty))$, $\pi_0(U(\infty))=0$, and $\pi_1(U(\infty))\cong\mathbb Z$.
editorial_note: Selects stable complex Bott periodicity; source separately describes real period-eight variant.

title: Brauer's theorem on induced characters
source_statement_excerpt: Brauer's theorem on induced characters, often known as Brauer's induction theorem, and named after Richard Brauer, is a basic result in the branch of mathematics known as character theory, which is part of the representation theory of finite groups.
editorial_note: Available excerpt only identifies Brauer's induction theorem by name and does not contain its actual claim.

title: Brillouin's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: The main consequence of the theorem arises when improving upon the Hartree-Fock approximation, a process known as including electronic correlation. Methods like configuration interaction (CI) build a more accurate wavefunction by combining the ground state with various excited states. Brillouin's theorem implies that when performing a CI calculation, all contributions from singly excited states will be zero. Therefore, to improve the Hartree-Fock energy, one only needs to consider states where two or more electrons have been excited, which significantly reduces the computational complexity. Mathematically, the theorem states that the matrix element of the Hamiltonian ${\hat {H}}$ between the ground state Hartree–Fock wavefunction $|\psi _{0}\rangle $ and a singly excited determinant $|\psi _{a}^{r}\rangle $ (i.e. one where an occupied orbital a is replaced by a virtual orbital r) is zero: $\langle \psi _{0}|{\hat {H}}|\psi _{a}^{r}\rangle =0$ This theorem is important in constructing a configuration interaction method, among other applications.
statement: For a Hartree–Fock reference determinant $\lvert\psi_0\rangle$ and any singly excited determinant $\lvert\psi_a^r\rangle$, the Hamiltonian matrix element $\langle\psi_0\lvert\widehat H\rvert\psi_a^r\rangle$ vanishes.
hypotheses: $\lvert\psi_0\rangle$ is a Hartree–Fock stationary reference determinant and $\lvert\psi_a^r\rangle$ differs from it by a single occupied-to-virtual orbital excitation.
conclusions: $\langle\psi_0\lvert\widehat H\rvert\psi_a^r\rangle=0$.
editorial_note: Statement drawn from formula in lead, not claim about every CI coefficient.

title: Brunn–Minkowski theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let n ≥ 1 and let μ denote the Lebesgue measure on Rn. Let A and B be two nonempty compact subsets of Rn. Then the following inequality holds: $[\mu (A+B)]^{1/n}\geq [\mu (A)]^{1/n}+[\mu (B)]^{1/n},$
statement: For nonempty compact sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $\mu(A+B)^{1/n}\ge\mu(A)^{1/n}+\mu(B)^{1/n}$.
hypotheses: $n\ge1$; $A,B$ are nonempty compact subsets of $\mathbb R^n$; $\mu$ is Lebesgue measure and $A+B$ their Minkowski sum.
editorial_note: Uses the exact source version for compact sets.

title: Burke's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: The departure process is a Poisson process with rate parameter λ.
statement: For a stationary $M/M/1$, $M/M/c$, or $M/M/\infty$ queue with Poisson arrival rate $\lambda$, the departure process is Poisson with rate $\lambda$, and the number in the system at time $t$ is independent of earlier departures.
hypotheses: The queue is a stationary $M/M/1$, $M/M/c$, or $M/M/\infty$ system with Poisson arrival rate $\lambda$.
conclusions: The departure process is a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$.
For each time $t$, the number of customers at time $t$ is independent of the departures before $t$.
editorial_note: Both bullet conclusions recovered from lead.

title: Butterfly theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let M be the midpoint of a chord PQ of a circle, through which two other chords AB and CD are drawn; AD and BC intersect chord PQ at X and Y correspondingly. Then M is the midpoint of XY.
statement: If $M$ is the midpoint of chord $PQ$ of a circle, chords $AB$ and $CD$ through $M$ meet cross-connections $AD$ and $BC$ at $X,Y$ on $PQ$, then $M$ is the midpoint of $XY$.
hypotheses: $P,Q,A,B,C,D$ lie on a circle; $M$ is midpoint of chord $PQ$; chords $AB,CD$ pass through $M$; lines $AD,BC$ intersect $PQ$ at $X,Y$ respectively.
conclusions: $MX=MY$.
editorial_note: Preserves named intersections from source.

title: Cantor's isomorphism theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In order theory and model theory, branches of mathematics, Cantor's isomorphism theorem states that every two nonempty countable dense unbounded linear orders are order-isomorphic.
statement: Any two nonempty countable dense linear orders without endpoints are order-isomorphic.
hypotheses: $L_1,L_2$ are nonempty countable linearly ordered sets, densely ordered and without a least or greatest element.
conclusions: There is an order-preserving bijection $L_1\to L_2$.
editorial_note: 'Unbounded' normalized to without endpoints.

title: Carathéodory kernel theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let fn(z) be a sequence of holomorphic univalent functions on the unit disk D, normalised so that fn(0) = 0 and f 'n (0) > 0. Then fn converges uniformly on compacts in D to a function f if and only if Un = fn(D) converges to its kernel and this kernel is not C. If the kernel is $\{0\}$ , then f = 0. Otherwise the kernel is a connected open set U, f is univalent on D and f(D) = U.
statement: For normalized univalent holomorphic maps $f_n:\mathbb D\to\mathbb C$, compact convergence of $f_n$ is equivalent to convergence of their image domains to a kernel other than $\mathbb C$, with the degenerate kernel giving the zero function and a nondegenerate kernel giving a univalent limiting map onto it.
hypotheses: $f_n$ is holomorphic and injective on $\mathbb D$, $f_n(0)=0$, $f_n'(0)>0$; $U_n=f_n(\mathbb D)$, and kernel convergence is as defined for domains containing $0$.
conclusions: $f_n$ converges locally uniformly on $\mathbb D$ to $f$ if and only if $(U_n)$ converges to its kernel $U$ and $U\ne\mathbb C$.
If $U=\{0\}$ then $f=0$; otherwise $U$ is connected and open, $f$ is univalent, and $f(\mathbb D)=U$.
editorial_note: Keeps source's non-$\mathbb C$ kernel condition and degeneration alternatives.

title: Casey's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $\,O$ be a circle of radius $\,R$ . Let $\,O_{1},O_{2},O_{3},O_{4}$ be (in that order) four non-intersecting circles that lie inside $\,O$ and tangent to it. Denote by $\,t_{ij}$ the length of the exterior common bitangent of the circles $\,O_{i},O_{j}$ . Then: $\,t_{12}\cdot t_{34}+t_{14}\cdot t_{23}=t_{13}\cdot t_{24}.$
statement: Four pairwise disjoint circles internally tangent to a containing circle satisfy $t_{12}t_{34}+t_{14}t_{23}=t_{13}t_{24}$, where $t_{ij}$ is the length of the exterior common bitangent of circles $i,j$.
hypotheses: $O_1,O_2,O_3,O_4$ are four pairwise nonintersecting circles in that cyclic order, lying inside and tangent to a circle $O$; $t_{ij}$ denotes exterior common bitangent length.
editorial_note: Retains order and bitangent convention from source.

title: Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let K denote the field of real or of complex numbers, and let V = Km and W = Kn. Let A1, ..., An−1 be analytic functions defined on some neighbourhood of (0, 0) in W × V and taking values in the m × m matrices, and let b be an analytic function with values in V defined on the same neighbourhood. Then there is a neighbourhood of 0 in W on which the quasilinear Cauchy problem
statement: A quasilinear first-order Cauchy problem with coefficients analytic near the origin and zero data on $x_n=0$ has a unique analytic local solution near the origin.
hypotheses: $K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $V=K^m$, $W=K^n$; analytic matrix-valued $A_1,\ldots,A_{n-1}$ and analytic $V$-valued $b$ are defined near $(0,0)\in W\times V$.
The Cauchy problem is $\partial_{x_n}f=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}A_j(x,f)\partial_{x_j}f+b(x,f)$ with initial data $f(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},0)=0$.
conclusions: There is a unique analytic solution $f$ on a neighborhood of $0\in W$.
editorial_note: Adjacent formulas supply PDE and zero initial condition.

title: Cauchy's theorem (group theory)
source_statement_excerpt: Integers ( $\mathbb {Z} $ )
editorial_note: The retrieved excerpt is an unrelated navigation list of groups; no theorem statement available.

title: Cayley's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: When G is finite, $\operatorname {Sym} (G)$ is finite too. The proof of Cayley's theorem in this case shows that if G is a finite group of order n, then G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the standard symmetric group $S_{n}$ . But G might also be isomorphic to a subgroup of a smaller symmetric group, $S_{m}$ for some $m<n$ ; for instance, the order 6 group $G=S_{3}$ is not only isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_{6}$ , but also (trivially) isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_{3}$ . The problem of finding the minimal-order symmetric group into which a given group G embeds is rather difficult.
statement: Every group $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group on its underlying set via left multiplication.
hypotheses: $G$ is a group and $\operatorname{Sym}(G)$ is its full permutation group.
conclusions: The map $g\mapsto (x\mapsto gx)$ is an injective group homomorphism $G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}(G)$.
editorial_note: Uses main theorem from preceding lead rather than incidental selected paragraph.

title: Ceva's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In Euclidean geometry, Ceva's theorem is a theorem about triangles. Given a triangle △ABC, let the lines AO, BO, CO be drawn from the vertices to a common point O (not on one of the sides of △ABC), to meet opposite sides at D, E, F respectively. (The segments AD, BE, CF are known as cevians.) Then, using signed lengths of segments,
statement: For triangle $ABC$ with points $D\in BC$, $E\in CA$, $F\in AB$, the cevians $AD,BE,CF$ are concurrent or all parallel if and only if the signed ratios satisfy $\frac{\overline{AF}}{\overline{FB}}\frac{\overline{BD}}{\overline{DC}}\frac{\overline{CE}}{\overline{EA}}=1$.
hypotheses: $A,B,C$ form a nondegenerate triangle; $D,E,F$ lie respectively on the lines $BC,CA,AB$, with signed segment ratios defined and nonzero denominators.
conclusions: $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent or all parallel if and only if $\frac{\overline{AF}}{\overline{FB}}\frac{\overline{BD}}{\overline{DC}}\frac{\overline{CE}}{\overline{EA}}=1$.
editorial_note: Includes converse's all-parallel alternative as described in adjacent excerpt.
